strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: to the authors' credit they carefully position the work against Adibi et al. (2022, convex-submodular) and Mualem et al. (2024, integer problems), and the non-smooth submodular-concave mixed-integer min-max setting appears genuinely unstudied.

The structural analysis is thoughtful: the discussion of when a saddle point exists for f versus its Lovász extension (Props. 2.10-2.11, Examples B.1/B.3, Remark B.2 on mixed-strategy Nash interpretation) is a valuable contribution beyond the algorithm itself, and the paper is honest that saddle-point existence for f is not automatic.

The offline (Theorem 3.2, O(nm²ε⁻²) queries) and online (Theorem 3.6, O(√(NP̄_N)) duality gap with path length) guarantees are stated with explicit hyperparameter choices, and full proofs are provided in Appendix C; the analysis correctly exploits subgradient structure of the Lovász extension in x and Gaussian smoothing only in y, with a justified cost argument (Remark D.1).

The online analysis handles the non-stationary oracle carefully: the 4-query vs 3-query variants (Remarks D.2-D.4) and the non-vanishing O(NV) error term are honest and informative about what is achievable in the online setting.

Extensive numerical illustration covering offline/online adversarial segmentation and clustering, with implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, run-to-run variance) that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the algorithm is a fairly direct combination of the Lovász-extension subgradient method (Hazan & Kale, 2012), Nesterov-Spokoiny Gaussian smoothing, and the extragradient method (Nedić-Ozdaglar, Farzin et al. 2025a). The rates (O(ε⁻²) offline, path-length online bounds) match standard subgradient/extragradient analyses, and much of the machinery is adapted from the authors' own prior work; the main novelty is assembling these for the submodular-concave class.

The final ε-saddle point guarantee (19) is via an argmin over generated iterates of the duality gap Dτ, which requires computing max_y f(S,y) and min_S f(S,y) at every iterate to implement the selection step; the paper does not discuss the oracle cost or practicality of this selection, which weakens the practical force of the theorem.

Per-iteration cost is 6n function evaluations, so total complexity is O(nm²ε⁻²); the linear dependence on n inherited from Lovász-extension subgradients limits scalability to large ground sets, and the paper does not benchmark against any alternative (e.g., first-order methods where supergradients are available, or cutting-plane/Frank-Wolfe-style SFM approaches) even in the experiments.

The experimental comparison in Table 1 is potentially unfair/ambiguous: both U-Nets are 'trained and evaluated without adversaries' while Algorithm 1 is evaluated under adversarial perturbation on the same video, yet adversarial robustness is listed as a differentiator; the text is contradictory about whether baselines see the adversarial video, so the claimed superiority is hard to interpret. All experiments are small synthetic instances (50×50 images, 40-50 point two-moons), so the significance of the empirical results is modest.

Several presentation defects: typos ('Costum', 'Minmiser', 'extragrdient', 'attacker Budget$'), and equation (30) on page 14 appears mis-stated (the second identity reads min_x max_y f^L = max_y min_S f(S,y), which is presumably meant to be min_S max_y f(S,y)); equation numbering and notation (D^L vs D_τ, index sets) are dense and occasionally inconsistent.

The existence-of-saddle-point assumption on f is maintained throughout the theory, but the conditions in Proposition 2.11 that guarantee it are restrictive (e.g., ζ(x) itself being a Lovász extension, or a common vertex minimiser); the paper does not discuss how frequently these hold in the experimental applications, leaving a gap between theory and practice.

No code release is mentioned, which, combined with the sensitive hyperparameter tuning acknowledged in Appendix E (accuracy 'is sensitive to the rate of change in the cost functions'), makes independent reproduction of the numerical claims non-trivial.

strengths: The problem setting—non-smooth submodular-concave min-max problems over mixed integer (set) and continuous variables—is reasonably novel; the authors make a credible case that this gap exists relative to Adibi et al. (2022) and Mualem et al. (2024).
The paper treats both offline and online regimes and provides explicit hyperparameter selections and a per-iteration query-cost accounting (Remark 3.3), which is more complete than many ZO papers.
Propositions 2.10-2.11 and Appendix B honestly delineate when saddle points of (1) exist and when solving the Lovász-extension relaxation (7) is valid, including worked counterexamples.
The online analysis via path length (Theorem 3.6) connects to established dynamic-regret style bounds, and Appendix D discusses relaxations of the function-query assumption between cost changes.
Limitations of the experimental comparison (e.g., sensitivity to the rate of cost change, role of the adversarial budget ρ) are discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The headline claim of converging to an ε-saddle point of the original mixed-integer problem (1) is overstated. The guarantee in Theorem 3.2 (eq. 19) is for the averaged/threshold gap D_τ, which essentially equals the duality gap of the Lovász extension (7); the actual duality gap of the returned integer set S̄_N (i.e., max_y f(S̄_N, y) − min_S f(S, ȳ_N)) is never bounded except under the restrictive conditions of Proposition 2.11 (e.g., a common vertex minimiser). The reduction from approximate minimisers of f^L to approximate solutions of (1) in the min-max setting is not established, so the central claim is not fully supported.

Existence of a saddle point for (1) is simply assumed, and the sufficient conditions offered are strong and hard to verify in practice; without them the algorithm may be solving a relaxation whose solution does not correspond to (1).

The online duality gap bound O(√(N P̄_N)) is unsatisfying: the benchmark sequence z̄_k in Theorem 3.6 is defined in terms of the algorithm's own iterates (via x̂_k, ŷ_k), making the path-length quantity partially self-referential; the practical meaning of this bound is unclear and not compared against existing online min-max baselines.

The complexity O(nm²ε⁻²) is not contextualised: when f is smooth or has accessible subgradients in y (as in the authors' own segmentation and clustering examples), first-order primal-dual methods would avoid the m² ZO penalty. No first-order or other baseline algorithm is implemented or compared, so the practical value of the ZO approach is not demonstrated.

The empirical evaluation is weak: only synthetic 50×50 two-segment images and a 50-point two-moons clustering. The comparison to U-Nets trained on 3000 rotations of a single base image is not a meaningful baseline, and the evaluation protocol is confusing—the U-Nets are 'trained and evaluated without adversaries' while Table 1 credits Algorithm 1 with adversarial robustness, making the comparison uninformative or unfair. No code is released, hindering reproducibility.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: numerous typos ('Costum', 'extragrdient', 'Minmiser', 'Submodluar', stray '$' in Figure 9), a garbled hyperparameter expression for N in Theorem 3.2, and the L0 = min{L0x, 4M} construction mixing two different boundedness arguments is sloppy.

The contribution is largely an assembly of known tools—the extragradient ZO framework of Farzin et al. (2025a), Lovász-extension subgradients from Hazan & Kale (2012), and Gaussian smoothing from Nesterov & Spokoiny (2017)—applied to a new problem class, without a technically deep new ingredient; the analysis mostly adapts standard extragradient telescope arguments.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: to the authors' (plausible) knowledge, no prior work provides algorithms with guarantees for non-smooth submodular-concave max-min/min-min problems, in contrast to the convex-submodular case (Adibi et al., 2022) and integer submodular min-max (Mualem et al., 2024). The distinction that submodular minimisation via the Lovász extension is fundamentally different from submodular maximisation is correctly drawn and motivates the setting.

The algorithmic design is well-motivated: using the subgradient of the Lovász extension for the set variable (avoiding the extra factor-2 cost of Gaussian smoothing in x, justified in Remark D.1) and a Gaussian two-point oracle for y is a sensible hybrid, and the per-iteration cost analysis in Remark 3.3 (6n evaluations per iteration, O(nm²ε⁻²) total) is transparent.

Complete proofs of all main results are provided in the appendix, and the analysis follows a defensible template: extragradient descent steps with non-expansive projections, Nesterov–Spokoiny bounds on the smoothed oracle, and standard Sion/minimax machinery for the convex-concave Lovász extension problem (7). The online result O(√(N P̄_N)) duality gap with path-length dependence is consistent with the dynamic-regret literature.

The paper is honest about structural subtleties: Propositions 2.10–2.11 explicitly characterise when a saddle point of f exists and when solving (7) recovers a solution of (1), with illustrative examples both with and without saddle points (Appendix B), including the interesting observation linking Lovász-extension solutions to mixed-strategy Nash equilibria.
The relaxation of the four-query assumption to three queries with an explicit extra error term O(NV) (Remarks D.2–D.4) shows the authors thought carefully about the online oracle design.

A breadth of experiments (offline/online adversarial segmentation, offline/online adversarial semi-supervised clustering) with ablations over the adversarial budget ρ, and an honest discussion of the robustness–accuracy trade-off and of non-monotone cost behaviour in the min-max regime.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the contribution is essentially a careful combination of three known ingredients — the Lovász-extension subgradient (Hazan & Kale, 2012), Gaussian-smoothed ZO oracles (Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017), and the extragradient/subgradient saddle-point scheme (Nedic & Ozdaglar, 2009; Farzin et al., 2025a, by largely the same authors on nonconvex-nonconcave problems). The analysis follows these templates closely, and the rates obtained (O(ε⁻²) offline, path-length online bounds) are the expected ones rather than exploiting the submodular structure for any improvement.

The central reduction is only conditionally valid. Solving (7) yields an ε-saddle point of f (the discrete problem of interest) only under the restrictive conditions of Proposition 2.11 (e.g., a common vertex minimiser across y ∈ Y, or ζ(x) itself a Lovász extension). The general guarantee (19) is stated in terms of D_τ, the threshold-averaged gap, not the discrete duality gap of (1). This gap between the analysed quantity and the claimed contribution is not fully resolved, and it is not verified in the experiments whether these structural conditions hold for the segmentation/clustering objectives.

The ε-saddle point guarantee is only in expectation over the random threshold τ (and the Gaussian samples). A high-probability statement, or a procedure to round the fractional minimiser to an actual set S with a certified gap, would be needed to make the guarantee actionable; the connection via Axelrod et al. (2020) is cited but the additional cost/concentration requirements are not analysed in the min-max setting.

Theory–practice mismatch: the experiments use t_k = 10–20 averaging samples, step sizes and µ that are hand-tuned and far from the theoretically prescribed hyperparameters, which depend on unknown constants (L0, L0y, M) and, in Theorem 3.6, on the unknown path length P̄_N (also noted as a limitation). The theorems are therefore not directly validated by the experiments.

The U-Net comparison in Table 1 is not a fair test of the headline claim. The U-Nets are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 is evaluated under adversarial perturbation, yet the table's 'Adversarial robustness: Yes/No' row is used to conclude superiority. Moreover, the semi-supervised U-Net receives the same seed inputs but no adversary, so the comparison conflates robustness by design with an unequal evaluation protocol. The experiments are also confined to synthetic 50×50 images and a 50-point two-moons dataset, limiting external validity.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned, hyperparameter selection is only partially documented (Appendix E lists values but not tuning procedures), and several constants needed to implement the theoretical step-size rules are not estimated anywhere.

Presentation is sloppy in places: undefined symbol L in the hyperparameter choices of Theorem 3.2 (L² vs L0²), L0 = min{L0x, 4M} where a max-like bound is expected, typos in equations ((45) mixes f^L(x, ẑk) with ẑ notation) and text ('extragrdient', 'Costum', 'Minmiser'), and awkward index/notation handling around (19) and the definition of (S̄_N, ȳ_N). These do not undermine the mathematics but suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

Significance is modest for a main-track paper: the algorithm and guarantees will primarily interest the submodular-optimisation and ZO communities, the application scenarios are small-scale and synthetic, and the future-work list (weak submodularity, unbounded sets, Nash interpretation) effectively concedes that the current results are a first step rather than a definitive treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new problem class: offline and online min-max optimization with non-smooth submodular-concave objectives. Prior work (Adibi et al. 2022 on convex-submodular, Mualem et al. 2024 on integer min-max) does not cover this setting, so the 'first study' claim appears well-founded and the paper carefully distinguishes itself from convex-submodular cases.

The theoretical development is coherent and mostly careful: the reduction to the Lovász extension (Lemma 2.7), the analysis of when saddle points of f exist and coincide with solutions of the relaxed problem (Propositions 2.10–2.11, with honest counterexamples in Appendix B), and the rounding argument via uniform threshold sampling are all handled rigorously.

The proofs in Appendix C are complete and contain non-trivial technical work beyond a routine combination of known results, e.g., the auxiliary-sequence argument (following Nemirovski et al.) to bound the sup over z in expectation for the duality gap (equations (45)-(50)), and the online analysis tracking the moving saddle point via path length.

The online duality gap O(√(N(1+P̄))) result is consistent with established behavior in online optimization, and the discussion of relaxing the four-query-per-function-change assumption (Appendix D, Remarks D.3-D.4) with the extra O(NV) error term is a useful and honest refinement.

Experiments cover both the offline and online regimes across three applications (adversarial segmentation offline/online, adversarial semi-supervised clustering offline/online), with hyperparameters reported, multiple runs (variance ~1e-4), an explicit robustness-accuracy trade-off study versus the adversary budget ρ (Figure 9), and a comparison table against trained U-Net baselines.

Limitations are candidly acknowledged: sensitivity of accuracy and tuning to the rate of change of the cost function (Appendix E.2), and the caveat that the U-Net baselines are trained and evaluated without adversaries while the comparison focuses on the strict online, adversarial, resource-constrained regime.
weaknesses: The algorithmic technique is largely a combination of established ingredients: the extragradient framework, Gaussian-smoothed two-point ZO oracles (Nesterov & Spokoiny), and subgradients of the Lovász extension (Hazan & Kale). The convergence analysis closely parallels Nesterov & Spokoiny and Nedić & Ozdaglar; the main novelty is the adaptation to the structured problem class rather than new proof techniques or fundamentally new algorithmic ideas.

The guarantee that the returned discrete pair is an ε-saddle point is weaker than it first appears: equation (19) shows D_τ(S̄_N, ȳ_N) ≤ ε where D_τ involves max_y E_τ[f(S̄_N, y)] — i.e., the gap holds only in expectation over the uniformly sampled threshold τ, not for the worst-case (or even the realized) discrete set. The practical significance of an expected-over-τ saddle point guarantee deserves more discussion.

The central assumption that a saddle point of f exists, with condition (10) (min over the hypercube equals min over vertices for the max), is restrictive and generally not verifiable a priori. Proposition 2.11 gives sufficient conditions (e.g., ζ(x) is itself a Lovász extension, or common vertex minimiser) that are somewhat ad hoc, and the experiments never verify whether (10) holds for the applied problems (segmentation, clustering).

Per-iteration cost is 6n function evaluations (Remark 3.3) and total complexity O(nm²ε⁻²) scales linearly in the ground-set size; all experiments are small-scale (50×50 images, 40-50 point clustering), so scalability to realistic segmentation or clustering problems is not demonstrated. The claimed real-time 60 fps operation is only shown on these tiny instances.

The comparison in Table 1 is methodologically uneven: the U-Net baselines are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 is 'robust by design' and evaluated under adversarial perturbations. Although the paper frames the comparison as evaluating the strict online adversarial regime, the headline claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' trained U-Nets is not an apples-to-apples result and could overstate practical significance.

The online result requires a known deterministic upper bound P̄ on the path length to set the step size h2; such a bound is generally unavailable in practice, and the paper offers only a brief justification that a trivial bound always exists. No experiment validates the O(√(N(1+P̄))) rate.

Numerous minor presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Submodluar' in Appendix B heading, 'C. Proof of Lemmas, Propositions, and Theorems' in the section title, 'minx∈{0,1}n f f L' in (30) on page 14, inconsistent bracket '∈ [0,1]' vs '[0, 1]'), an incomplete URL in the reference (Farzin et al., 2025a), and a stray '23' after the CPU specification in Appendix E. Several cited works are arXiv preprints or self-citations of the authors' own ZO line of work.

The dependence of the y-update on the Lovász extension value f^L(x,y), which itself requires n function evaluations per call, means the ZO oracle cost is tied to n; the paper argues this is optimal given Remark D.1, but an empirical ablation (e.g., t_k sensitivity, effect of n) is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem class: non-smooth submodular-concave min-max problems, in both offline and online settings, and claims (plausibly) to be the first systematic ZO treatment of this combination.

The theoretical development is careful and complete. The offline analysis (Theorem 3.2) gives an ε-saddle point guarantee with explicit hyperparameter choices, and the online analysis (Theorem 3.6) yields an O(√(N(1+P̄))) duality gap consistent with classical dynamic-regret behaviour. The appendices contain full proofs, including a non-trivial extension of the Nemirovski et al. auxiliary-sequence technique to handle the correlated oracle noise in the extragradient setting (eqs. 46-50).

The paper is honest about the subtleties: Propositions 2.10-2.11 explicitly characterise when a saddle point exists and when solving the relaxed problem (7) recovers a solution of (1), and Appendix B gives concrete examples both with and without saddle points. Appendix D carefully discusses relaxing the four-query assumption and the extra error term O(NV) that arises.

The numerical section spans four settings (offline/online segmentation, offline/online clustering) with reasonable implementation detail, hyperparameters, and an honest discussion of the adversarial budget ρ and its robustness-accuracy trade-off.

The discussion of limitations is genuine (e.g., sensitivity of accuracy to the rate of change of the cost function, per Remark D.4), and the comparison table does not hide that U-Net baselines were evaluated without adversaries.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely a synthesis of known components: the extragradient/ZO machinery is taken from Farzin et al. (2025a) and Nesterov & Spokoiny (2017), the Lovász extension subgradient oracle from Hazan & Kale (2012), and the online path-length analysis follows Zinkevich (2003). The main novelty is the combination and the bookkeeping for the set-valued variable, which reduces the incremental feel of the results.

A central applicability concern: the algorithm solves the relaxation (7) and the guarantees (Theorem 3.2, eq. 19; Theorem 3.6, eq. 26) are stated for the threshold-averaged quantity E_τ[f(S_τ, y)], i.e., for the Lovász-relaxed duality gap, not for the original integer problem (1). Recovery of a genuine discrete ε-saddle point of (1) requires the restrictive conditions of Proposition 2.11 (e.g., a common vertex minimiser or vertex minimisers of ζ). For the adversarial segmentation/clustering instances in Section 4 and Appendix E, no verification is offered that these conditions hold, so the theory may not actually certify the behaviour observed in the experiments.

The headline empirical claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' supervised and semi-supervised U-Nets (Table 1) is not persuasive: the U-Nets are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 runs in the adversarial regime, no adversarially-trained baseline is included, and the domain is tiny synthetic 50x50 two-segment images. This comparison says more about the experimental design than about the merits of the method.

Scalability is a concern that the paper does not confront: each iteration requires ~6n function evaluations (Remark 3.3), giving O(nm²ε⁻²) total queries with a per-iteration cost linear in n. For the 2500-pixel images used, this implies ~15,000 function evaluations per iteration, which sits awkwardly with the claimed ~80 fps real-time performance; no profiling or wall-clock breakdown is provided.

The online guarantees require knowledge of an upper bound P̄ on the path length of optimal decisions to set the step sizes, and the resulting bound O(√(N(1+P̄))) is vacuous when P̄ grows linearly; the paper does not discuss how restrictive this is in practice.

Presentation has a number of loose ends: the oracle (14) is a smoothed estimate but the subgradient g_x is exact only up to the sampled chain/threshold coupling; the dependency between the threshold sampling and the function-value oracle in (8) is glossed over; several typos and notation inconsistencies (e.g., f^L_μ vs. ∇y f^L_{kμ} in (23), 'P^N_{k=0}' summation limits) reduce polish. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the experimental claims.

The 'first study' claim, while defensible in the narrow non-smooth submodular-concave setting, sits close to prior work on convex-submodular min-max (Adibi et al., 2022), submodular integer min-max (Mualem et al., 2024), and ZO extragradient min-max (Farzin et al., 2025a); the positioning could better delineate what is technically new beyond the combined setting.

strengths: The paper addresses a problem that appears genuinely unstudied: non-smooth submodular-concave min-max/max-min problems in both offline and online regimes, with a clear identification of the gap relative to (Adibi et al., 2022) (convex-submodular) and (Mualem et al., 2024) (submodular integer min-max).

The theoretical treatment is careful and unusually honest about structural issues: Proposition 2.10/2.11 and Appendix B explicitly characterize when a saddle point of f exists versus when only the Lovász-extension relaxation (7) has a saddle point, including a worked example of a submodular-concave function without a saddle point and its mixed-strategy interpretation.

The main theorems (3.2, 3.6) come with complete proofs (Appendix C), including a nontrivial stochastic duality-gap argument via the auxiliary-sequence technique (Nemirovski et al., 2009) to handle the sup over z in (18)/(50), and an explicit per-iteration oracle-cost accounting (Remark 3.3, total O(nm²ε⁻²) queries).

Hyperparameter choices (µ, h1, h2, N) are given explicitly for both offline and online cases, and the online result's dependence on path length O(√(N(1+P̄))) is consistent with classical dynamic-regret behavior; Appendix D thoughtfully discusses relaxing the four-query assumption to three queries and the extra error term O(NV) that then appears.

The experimental section covers multiple settings (offline/online adversarial segmentation, offline/online adversarial semi-supervised clustering), reports implementation details and hyperparameters, and discusses limitations (sensitivity to the rate of cost-function change, per Appendix D).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the algorithm is essentially the extragradient method with a Lovász-extension subgradient for x (Hazan & Kale, 2012) and a Gaussian-smoothed ZO oracle for y (Nesterov & Spokoiny, 2017), closely following the authors' own prior work (Farzin et al., 2025a,c,d). The rate O(ε⁻²) matches the classical first-order subgradient result of Nedić–Ozdaglar (2009); no lower bounds are provided to assess whether the O(m²ε⁻²) complexity is meaningful or improvable.

The headline guarantee is weaker than it first appears: Theorem 3.2/3.6 bound a threshold-averaged gap Dτ (or Dual-Gapτ) involving Eτ[f(S̄N, y)], i.e., a randomized-rounding, expectation-based notion, rather than a duality gap evaluated at an actual set S̄N. Recovering a genuine saddle point of (1) additionally requires condition (10) (Prop. 2.11), which is only sufficient and may not hold. The abstract/intro do not clearly flag this restriction.

Per-iteration cost scales linearly in n (6n evaluations per iteration), so the total complexity O(nm²ε⁻²) is quite expensive for large ground sets; the paper does not compare against any baseline algorithm empirically (e.g., primal-dual subgradient or other ZO min-max methods), so the practical advantage of the proposed method is not established relative to alternatives.

The U-Net comparison in Table 1 is potentially misleading: the U-Nets are trained and evaluated without adversarial perturbations while Algorithm 1 is evaluated with adversaries, and the U-Net baselines were trained on only one base-image family on synthetic 50×50 data. The claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' trained U-Nets is therefore not a well-controlled comparison, and the paper's own Appendix E.2 concedes the baselines could be improved.

Experiments are small-scale and purely synthetic (50×50 images, 50–40-point clustering); there is no demonstration on realistic data despite the motivation citing real applications. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the U-Net training and video experiments.

Presentation quality is uneven: typos ('Submodluar', 'Lovasz Extension Minmiser', a stray '$' in the Figure 9 title), an incomplete reference entry ('Available at' with no URL), and raw-looking remarks in Appendix D suggest the manuscript needed another proofread.

The saddle-point existence assumption is imposed throughout the analysis ('we assume that a saddle point ... exists'), and the sufficient conditions of Proposition 2.11 are restrictive (e.g., common vertex minimiser), so the applicability of the theory to the motivating applications (adversarial segmentation/clustering) is not verified—the paper does not check whether the actual objective functions used in Section 4 satisfy condition (10).
